entries.name: NICK
entries.description: Nickel: density 8908 kg/m3, k=90.9 W/mK, melts 1455C. Corrosion-resistant ferromagnetic metal, good conductor.
entries.use: Corrosion-resistant plating/alloying metal (stainless, batteries, coinage); a good, cheap conductor between S316 and BRSS.

entries.name: ZINC
entries.description: Zinc: density 7140 kg/m3, k=116 W/mK, melts only 419.5C. Sacrificial anode metal (galvanizing) protects steel from rust.
entries.use: Low-melting galvanizing/anode metal; melts well below most structural metals here, into a generic breakable melt.

entries.name: TIN
entries.description: Tin: density 7310 kg/m3, k=66.8 W/mK, melts only 231.9C. Historic solder/bronze-alloy metal, very soft.
entries.use: Very low-melting solder metal; softest structural metal in the catalog, melts into a generic breakable melt.

entries.name: SLVR
entries.description: Silver: density 10490 kg/m3, k=429 W/mK (best of any metal), melts 961.8C. Best electrical/thermal conductor known.
entries.use: Best-in-class conductor for premium contacts/bus bars, ahead of copper and gold; melts far hotter than tin/zinc.

entries.name: CHRM
entries.description: Chromium: density 7190 kg/m3, k=93.9 W/mK, melts 1907C. One of the hardest pure metals; forms stainless steel's passive oxide.
entries.use: Very hard, corrosion-resistant plating/alloying metal (the Cr in stainless/chrome plating).

entries.name: COBT
entries.description: Cobalt: density 8900 kg/m3, k=100 W/mK, melts 1495C. Ferromagnetic; parent metal of the Co-60 isotope (see CO60).
entries.use: Ferromagnetic alloying metal for superalloys and magnets; irradiate it to imagine how CO60 is made.

entries.name: CS
entries.description: Cesium metal: density 1873 kg/m3, k=35.9 W/mK, melts at just 28.5C. The most reactive stable alkali metal. 2026-08-26: dT rebalanced 900->400 (below K's 800) to fix a real-energy ordering inversion.
entries.use: The alkali metal that melts in your hand; more reactive than NA/K/RBDM, this catalog's most dramatic 'melts near room temp' demo.

entries.name: K
entries.description: Potassium metal: density 862 kg/m3, k=102.4 W/mK, melts only 63.5C. Softer and more reactive than sodium.
entries.use: Even softer/lower-melting alkali metal than NA; melts into the same NaK-type liquid-alkali stand-in.

entries.name: CA
entries.description: Calcium metal: density 1550 kg/m3, k=201 W/mK, melts 842C. Alkaline-earth metal, much less reactive than Na/K but still tarnishes readily.
entries.use: Alkaline-earth structural/reducing metal; melts far hotter than the true alkalis, like a light-duty aluminium substitute.

entries.name: WP
entries.description: White phosphorus: density 1823 kg/m3, k=0.236 W/mK, melts 44.1C and spontaneously ignites in air above ~30C. Highly toxic.
entries.use: Pyrophoric waxy solid that catches fire almost the instant it warms past room temperature; also poisonous on contact.

entries.name: S
entries.description: Sulfur: density 2070 kg/m3, k=0.205 W/mK, melts 115.2C, ignites ~232C burning with a blue flame to SO2.
entries.use: Classic yellow brimstone; melts long before it ignites, then burns with sulfur's characteristic blue flame.

entries.name: MGRB
entries.description: Magnesium ribbon: same metal as MG but thin-gauge; ignites at ~610C (below its own 650C melting point) and burns dazzlingly white.
entries.use: Thin-strip magnesium that ignites before it melts thanks to high surface area, unlike the bulk MG ingot; classic flash/flare fuel.

entries.name: NE
entries.description: Neon gas: colourless, chemically inert noble gas, density 0.9 kg/m3 (STP), k=0.0491 W/mK. Glows orange-red in electrical discharge.
entries.use: Inert noble gas for neon-sign discharge tubes; boils into this from LNE at 27K.

entries.name: KR
entries.description: Krypton gas: colourless, inert noble gas, density 3.7 kg/m3 (STP), k=0.0095 W/mK. Glows greenish-white in discharge.
entries.use: Heavy inert noble gas used in high-efficiency lamps and window-pane insulation fill.

entries.name: XE
entries.description: Xenon gas: colourless, inert noble gas, density 5.9 kg/m3 (STP), k=0.0057 W/mK. Glows blue-violet in discharge (xenon lamps).
entries.use: Heaviest common noble gas, used in xenon arc lamps, ion-thruster propellant, and dark-matter detectors (see LXE).

entries.name: CL2
entries.description: Chlorine gas: pale yellow-green, density 3.2 kg/m3 (STP), k=0.0089 W/mK. Toxic in trace concentrations (WWI chemical weapon).
entries.use: Classic deadly gas used in water treatment, PVC feedstock, and historically as a weaponized asphyxiant.

entries.name: F2
entries.description: Fluorine gas: pale yellow, density 1.7 kg/m3 (STP), k=0.0277 W/mK. Most reactive/electronegative element known, extremely toxic and corrosive.
entries.use: The most aggressive halogen gas; also the boil-off product of liquid fluorine (LF2).

entries.name: NH3
entries.description: Ammonia gas: density 0.73 kg/m3 (STP), k=0.0246 W/mK. Narrow flammability range (15-28% by volume); cracks into N2+H2 above ~500C industrially.
entries.use: Refrigerant/fertiliser-feedstock gas; industrially cracked at high temperature to release hydrogen (HYGN) here.

entries.name: CH4
entries.description: Methane gas: density 0.657 kg/m3 (STP), k=0.0343 W/mK, autoignites ~537C. Main component of natural gas.
entries.use: Primary natural-gas fuel component; also the boil-off product of liquid methane (LCH4, real Titan-lake chemistry).

entries.name: PROP
entries.description: Propane gas: density 1.88 kg/m3 (STP), k=0.018 W/mK, autoignites ~470C. Liquefies under modest pressure (LPG).
entries.use: Bottled-gas (LPG) fuel; ignites at a somewhat lower temperature than methane.

entries.name: O3
entries.description: Ozone gas: pale blue, density 2.14 kg/m3 (STP), k=0.0157 W/mK. Unstable, decomposes to O2 readily on mild heating; toxic and can detonate at high concentration.
entries.use: Unstable, toxic triatomic oxygen allotrope that readily breaks back down into ordinary oxygen (OXYG) when warmed.

entries.name: KCL
entries.description: Potassium chloride: density 1984 kg/m3, k=6.4 W/mK, melts 770C. Salt substitute and fertiliser feedstock.
entries.use: Potash salt used in fertiliser and low-sodium salt substitutes; a saltier-tasting cousin of NaCl (SALT).

entries.name: CACL
entries.description: Calcium chloride (anhydrous): density 2150 kg/m3, k=1.08 W/mK, melts 772C. Strongly hygroscopic road-salt/desiccant.
entries.use: Hygroscopic de-icing salt/desiccant, much more moisture-hungry than ordinary NaCl.

entries.name: LIF
entries.description: Lithium fluoride: density 2640 kg/m3, k=11.3 W/mK (unusually high for an ionic salt), melts 848C. Used in optics and molten-salt reactor fuel carriers.
entries.use: Unusually heat-conductive ionic salt for UV optics windows and molten-salt reactor fluoride carriers.

entries.name: MGO
entries.description: Magnesium oxide (magnesia): density 3580 kg/m3, k=48 W/mK, melts 2852C. Extremely refractory ceramic insulator.
entries.use: Ultra-refractory electrical-insulator ceramic used to pack heating-element sheaths; hotter-melting than ALUM or ZRCA.

entries.name: CAF2
entries.description: Calcium fluoride (fluorite): density 3180 kg/m3, k=9.7 W/mK, melts 1418C. Natural mineral, transparent to UV/IR.
entries.use: Natural fluorite mineral valued for UV/IR-transparent optics windows and as a flux in steelmaking.

entries.name: NA2C
entries.description: Sodium carbonate (soda ash): density 2540 kg/m3, k=0.9 W/mK, melts 851C. Glassmaking flux and water softener.
entries.use: Soda-ash flux used in glass and detergent manufacture; melts well below the SDST/GRNT/BSLT it helps process.

entries.name: CNT
entries.description: Carbon nanotube (rolled graphene sheet): axial k up to ~3000-6000 W/mK, oxidizes in air ~3500C like graphite/graphene.
entries.use: Rolled-graphene tube, second only to GRPN for heat/electrical conduction; the fibrous cousin of that flat sheet.

entries.name: SOOT
entries.description: Amorphous carbon soot: disordered/porous carbon, k~0.1-0.2 W/mK, ignites ~427C (far lower than graphite thanks to huge surface area).
entries.use: Fluffy combustion-residue carbon; poorly conductive and far easier to ignite than any crystalline carbon allotrope here.

entries.name: C60
entries.description: Fullerene (Buckminsterfullerene C60): molecular carbon-cage crystal, k~0.4 W/mK, sublimes/oxidizes ~680C.
entries.use: Soccer-ball-shaped carbon-cage molecule; a poor conductor unlike CNT/GRPN despite being pure carbon.

entries.name: GAN
entries.description: Gallium nitride: density 6150 kg/m3, k=130 W/mK, wide-bandgap semiconductor that dissociates ~1200C at 1atm.
entries.use: Wide-bandgap power/RF semiconductor (fast chargers, RF amps); conducts even better than SIC or GAAS.

entries.name: CDTE
entries.description: Cadmium telluride: density 5850 kg/m3, k=6.2 W/mK, melts 1092C. ~20% efficient thin-film solar-cell semiconductor.
entries.use: Thin-film photovoltaic semiconductor, real-world ~20% panel efficiency; a cheaper, more toxic alternative to SIPV/GAAS.

entries.name: INP
entries.description: Indium phosphide: density 4810 kg/m3, k=68 W/mK, melts 1062C. High-speed RF/laser-diode semiconductor.
entries.use: High-frequency RF and laser-diode semiconductor, more conductive than GaAs or CdTe.

entries.name: U235
entries.description: Uranium-235 metal (enriched): fissile isotope, melts 1132C like natural uranium, but its neutron output here is tuned much faster than UO2's slow fuel-pellet fission.
entries.use: Weapons/reactor-grade fissile metal; a hotter neutron source than the UO2 fuel pellet, unclad and undiluted by oxide/zirconium.

entries.name: AM241
entries.description: Americium-241: density 13670 kg/m3, melts 1176C. Weak alpha/gamma emitter used as the ionization source in household smoke detectors.
entries.use: Weakly radioactive actinide, same isotope used in real smoke-detector ionization chambers; modeled as inert but flagged radioactive.

entries.name: CO60
entries.description: Cobalt-60: same metal as COBT (melts 1495C), but radioactive with a strong gamma-ray output; used in radiotherapy and industrial irradiators.
entries.use: Dedicated gamma-ray source (radiotherapy/food irradiation); emits photons rather than neutrons, unlike the fission sources above.

entries.name: TRIT
entries.description: Tritium gas (3H2): radioactive hydrogen isotope, beta emitter, half-life 12.3 years, flammable/explosive like ordinary hydrogen.
entries.use: Radioactive hydrogen isotope gas used in fusion-boosted weapons and self-luminous exit signs; decays away over time like a real half-life.

entries.name: B10
entries.description: Boron-10 powder: stable (non-radioactive) isotope with one of the highest thermal-neutron capture cross-sections known, even better than natural cadmium.
entries.use: Best-in-class neutron-poison powder, absorbs even more reliably than HF/CD/B4C; a stable isotope, not itself radioactive.

entries.name: CF252
entries.description: Californium-252: melts 900C, extremely potent spontaneous-fission neutron source used to start up nuclear reactors.
entries.use: The most intense neutron source in this catalog; used in reality as a portable reactor-startup/well-logging neutron source.

entries.name: RA226
entries.description: Radium-226: melts 700C, alpha/gamma emitter historically used in glow-in-the-dark radium paint before its dangers were understood.
entries.use: The original radioluminescent element; pulses with a slow visible glow rather than emitting particles, echoing old radium-dial paint.

entries.name: CELL
entries.description: Cellulose: plant-cell-wall polysaccharide, k~0.2 W/mK, autoignites ~232C (the 'Fahrenheit 451' paper-burning temperature).
entries.use: The structural fibre of paper/cotton/wood; ignites at the famous 232C paper autoignition temperature.

entries.name: LIGN
entries.description: Lignin: the char-forming aromatic polymer binding wood fibres, k~0.2-0.4 W/mK, ignites ~297C. 2026-08-26: chance lowered 0.2->0.12 (was byte-identical to CELL's rule, a bug) so it now actually ignites harder than pure cellulose as its own text claims.
entries.use: Wood's binding polymer; chars rather than flaming as readily as pure cellulose, harder to ignite.

entries.name: CHIT
entries.description: Chitin: structural polysaccharide of insect/crustacean exoskeletons and fungal cell walls, k~0.3-0.5 W/mK, ignites ~317C.
entries.use: Tough natural biopolymer forming shells/exoskeletons; more rigid and slower-burning than plant cellulose.

entries.name: BONE
entries.description: Cortical bone (hydroxyapatite + collagen): k~0.4-0.6 W/mK, chars and calcines to bone ash by ~600C rather than burning outright.
entries.use: Mineralized skeletal tissue; low flammability, calcines into a stony ash residue instead of flaming like pure organics.

entries.name: KERA
entries.description: Keratin: structural protein of hair/horn/nail/feather, k~0.05 W/mK (very insulating), ignites easily around 195C with a characteristic smell.
entries.use: Hair/horn/nail protein; among the best natural insulators here, but ignites at a lower temperature than the plant fibres.

entries.name: SUGR
entries.description: Sucrose (table sugar): k~0.58 W/mK, caramelizes ~180C then chars/burns ~362C. Fine sugar dust is a known industrial explosion hazard.
entries.use: Common crystalline sugar; also a real combustible-dust hazard, so it carries a small explosive rating alongside flammability.

entries.name: STAR
entries.description: Starch (amylose/amylopectin): granular plant carbohydrate, ignites ~387C. Fine starch/flour dust is a classic combustible-dust (grain-mill) hazard.
entries.use: Granular plant-storage carbohydrate; like SUGR, its fine dust form carries real explosion risk.

entries.name: TLLW
entries.description: Tallow (rendered animal fat): solid at room temperature, ignites ~250C. Classic candle/soap fuel.
entries.use: Rendered animal fat, historically the main candle and soap fuel; ignites readily like the vegetable oils it resembles.

entries.name: BEES
entries.description: Beeswax: melts 62-64C, latent heat ~177 kJ/kg, flash point ~204C. A phase-change heat buffer, unlike petroleum-derived PCMP (paraffin).
entries.use: Natural-wax phase-change buffer, distinct from mineral-paraffin PCMP; soaks/releases heat at ~62C before eventually catching fire if overheated.

entries.name: LNE
entries.description: Liquid neon: density 1207 kg/m3, boils at 27.07K, k~0.114 W/mK. A niche cryogen used where liquid helium is overkill.
entries.use: Mid-range cryogen (colder than LN2, warmer than LHE) for cooling infrared detectors; boils back into NE gas.

entries.name: LAR
entries.description: Liquid argon: density 1400 kg/m3, boils at 87.3K, k~0.126 W/mK. The working fluid of real dark-matter/neutrino detectors.
entries.use: Detector-grade cryogenic liquid (as used in real dark-matter and neutrino experiments); boils back into the existing ARGN gas.

entries.name: LKR
entries.description: Liquid krypton: density 2413 kg/m3, boils at 119.75K, k~0.095 W/mK. Used as a dense calorimeter medium in particle physics.
entries.use: Dense cryogenic liquid used as an electromagnetic-calorimeter medium in particle detectors; boils into KR gas.

entries.name: LXE
entries.description: Liquid xenon: density 2942 kg/m3, boils at 165.05K, k~0.072 W/mK. The working fluid of the most sensitive real dark-matter detectors.
entries.use: The densest common cryogenic liquid here; the medium of choice for real ultra-sensitive dark-matter experiments. Boils into XE gas.

entries.name: LCH4
entries.description: Liquid methane: density 422.6 kg/m3, boils at 111.65K, k~0.191 W/mK, flammable. Fills the actual lakes of Titan and is used as rocket fuel (Raptor/Starship).
entries.use: Cryogenic rocket propellant (methalox) and the real liquid-lake fluid on Saturn's moon Titan; boils into CH4 gas.

entries.name: LF2
entries.description: Liquid fluorine: density 1505 kg/m3, boils at 85.03K, k~0.155 W/mK. Extremely corrosive/toxic cryogenic oxidizer, historically tested as a rocket propellant.
entries.use: Ferociously reactive cryogenic oxidizer, tested (and mostly abandoned) as a rocket propellant due to its extreme toxicity/corrosiveness. Boils into F2 gas.
